commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel (#9830)

The hero router's top-(K+1) expert selection runs in a Triton kernel
instead of a full XLA sort of every row: 0.096 ms per call instead of
0.856 ms at [65536, 384], k = 9 on one GB200, once in the forward and
again in the recompute. The indices and their order match
`jax.lax.top_k` bitwise for every input, including ties, signed zeros,
infinities and NaNs.

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024
elements, so 384-expert rows fall back to a sort. The new kernel takes
float32 rows narrower than 1,024 on a GPU device; everything else keeps
`jax.lax.top_k`. Its gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU,
because a hero test stubs `jax.default_backend` to trace a GPU-only path
on CPU devices. The Triton gather-sum's gate makes the same check.

One warp holds one row in registers, as one power-of-two tile or, when
that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide
tiles), and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order
key, breaking ties by the lower column. A row in one warp keeps both
reductions inside the warp; Triton reduces across warps through shared
memory. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n,
which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with
payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose key is also the smallest, is not mistaken for
one. The kernel reads an int32 view of the input, so autodiff never asks
it for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop, which
compiles in 0.2 s where unrolled steps take 36 s at k = 384.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore
step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that took 0.125 ms
per call shortened the step by 0.53%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

commits.author: dlwh
commits.message:
[iris] Document actor RPC trust and network isolation (#9913)

Actor RPC deserializes arguments, results, and exceptions with
cloudpickle. Clients must trust servers and servers must trust clients,
because deserializing these payloads can execute Python code. Document
the unauthenticated direct listener and code-execution trust delegated
by actor RPC endpoint links.

Direct listeners must stay on trusted networks. External controller
endpoint proxies must enforce authentication; null-auth proxies are
permissive and must also stay on trusted networks. Run untrusted jobs
with the sandbox profile and INTERNET or NONE egress. On Kubernetes,
these egress restrictions require the network plugin to enforce
NetworkPolicy. This change documents the existing boundary and does not
change runtime access controls.

Scoped repository lint and 28 existing actor, proxy-authentication, and
sandbox tests passed. Live cluster network enforcement was not tested.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel (#9829)

Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that
reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is
deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv`
to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block,
short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The
forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same
tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same
algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed
code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to
the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of
64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence
to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the
padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls
fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets
the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed;
checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in
bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90
and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`,
`add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which
rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot
contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback
has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80
GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the
previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of
dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step
before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A
step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts
a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore
step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15%
slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[experiments] Add a Slurm wrapper for the AMD HPC Fund cluster (#9877)

Add `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh`, a Slurm wrapper for Python
entry points on the AMD HPC Fund cluster (partitions `mi3508x` and
`mi3008x`), with a README covering submission, the ROCm 10 venv recipe
and known issues. `experiments/amd/` will also hold AMD experiments that
are not tied to this cluster.

The wrapper turns off XLA command buffers, which caused NaN gradients
and segfaults after a few steps on this ROCm stack. It also sets
`JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`, because JAX stores XLA's
per-fusion autotune results in the compilation cache directory. Reusing
those results across configurations produced executables 2-3x slower
(`save_moe` at batch 64: 4.95 s per step against 1.83 s) and a false
batch-96 regression. Values the caller sets in the environment take
precedence.

The wrapper leaves `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` unset, so Haliax picks the
implementation (Triton on GPU, falling back to XLA). The README asks
benchmark runs to set it explicitly so results stay comparable, and
notes that XLA's `ragged_dot` rejects bf16 on MI350X (gfx950). On
MI300X, XLA is the fastest path: in per-call microbenchmarks on one GPU,
its bf16 grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per forward+backward triple
than the best Triton configuration.

The results posted on #9812 so far used an earlier copy of this wrapper
at `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh` (git blob
`798795b2265f3ce6dd0e47f338b3c6ba6a826e53`). That copy defaulted
`RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` to `xla` and did not set the autotune-cache variable.
#9886 adds the collective benchmark under `experiments/amd/` and should
merge after this PR.

Part of #9812

commits.message:
[ci] Raise the levanter-tpu job timeout to 35 minutes (#9893)

Raise the `levanter-tpu` job timeout in `unified-unit.yaml` from 25 to
35
minutes, and the pytest `timeout` inside its container from 1490 to 2090
seconds. The inner timeout would otherwise stop pytest about 25.5
minutes into
the job, so raising only the job limit would add less than a minute.

The full Levanter TPU suite runs only on pull requests that touch
`levanter`,
`haliax`, or the CI selector. #9899 cut the time from job start to
pytest from
about 100 seconds to about 40 by hardlinking the venv from the uv cache.
The
suite still barely fits. The first `main` run after #9899

([113011520284](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/37685242488/job/113011520284))
selected 1837 tests, ran them in 23:21 (`1580 passed, 258 skipped`), and
finished in 24.0 minutes. That is 1 minute under the job limit and about
1.5
minutes under the pytest timeout.

Before #9899, 12 pull-request runs on October 2 and 3 were cancelled at
25.1
minutes. Each had reached 97-100% of the tests with no failures.

Faster setup does not remove the need for more time, because the suite
keeps
growing. In September the whole job passed in 18.7-19.4 minutes with
1541
selected tests. Today it selects 1837 tests, and the tests alone take
23.3
minutes. That is about 4.5 minutes of growth in a month. At that rate
the
current 1-minute margin lasts about a week, and a 35-minute limit lasts
about
two months.

A normal run costs nothing extra. A hung run can hold the TPU runner for
up to
10 more minutes. Splitting the suite across runners would fix the growth
for
longer, but that is a separate change.

Co-authored-by: Amy Sartran <users.noreply.github.com>

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails (#9895)

When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__`
sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed,
and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped
the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups
writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next
read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so
`atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the
fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

Co-authored-by: Rafal Wojdyla <ravwojdyla@gmail.com>

commits.message:
[finestore] Batch exact-query cache reads (#9876)

Batch TaskCompendium's exact-query cache probes once per Zephyr review
window, then submit only misses. Keep bounded Parquet readers and close
shard readers after use. Remove the local SQLite key index, whose cold
build scans remote descriptor shards on each worker.

Store named objects up to 128 KiB inline; larger values use parts of up
to 8 MiB. Read requested parts together and cap blob descriptor row
groups at 1,024 rows. Ordinary table row groups remain at 16,384, and
existing larger inline blobs remain readable. FineStore views and
persistent caches now accumulate read diagnostics automatically and
expose snapshots through `read_diagnostics()`. Finelog counters report
read volume and cache outcomes; histograms report read time and
descriptor-shard fanout.

In a synthetic GCS probe from this client host, a 100-name batch with 10
hits among 2,048 stored 4 KiB values took 3.84 and 3.07 seconds after
compaction to one shard. The 1,024-row limit has not shown a clear
latency gain over 16,384 for dispersed reads; 128-row groups were much
slower in the same sparse-hit setup. A separate 12 KiB probe used the
earlier 10 KiB inline cutoff and does not measure the current layout.
[The analysis and probe
details](https://loom.oa.dev/s/4kgvaf11/artifacts/finestore-cache-analysis)
describe the access path, limits, and next storage steps. CoreWeave S3
was unavailable from this session.

Part of #9497

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures (#9721)

Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent.
Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a
small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons
persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully
probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID,
report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions
fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared
cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and
`cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket
under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while
cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target
after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its
budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator
cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is
unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are
documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that
motivated this check is recorded in the [hero
incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

commits.message:
zephyr: give each worker attempt its own worker ID (#9741)

* fixes #9740
* zephyr worker ID now includes the iris attempt number:
`<group>-<index>-a<attempt_id>` (`attempt_worker_id`)
* iris can start a new attempt of a lost worker task while the old
attempt still runs; both used the same worker ID
* the old attempt pulled a shard after the new one registered, then
died, and the new attempt's heartbeats kept the shared ID alive, so the
shard stayed in flight forever [^1]
* with one ID per attempt, each process has its own liveness:
* a dead old attempt misses its heartbeats, and `check_heartbeats`
requeues its shards (up to the 120 s timeout)
* a live old attempt can finish its shards; the attempt check keeps the
current result
* no RPC changes; outside iris (`get_job_info()` is `None`) the attempt
is 0
* add
`test_shard_of_a_dead_replaced_attempt_is_requeued_while_its_successor_lives`,
which builds two `ZephyrWorker` attempts and fails with the shared ID
* side effects:
* dead attempts stay in the coordinator maps as `FAILED`, so the `N/M
workers alive, D dead` status line and the dashboard worker list grow
with each replaced attempt
* re-registration under the same ID now only covers a repeated
registration from the same process [^2]

[^1]: seen 3 times on 2026-10-04 in the datakit ferry runs (tier 1 and
tier 2), each after a preemptible v5e host was lost. The coordinator
showed `105/106 complete, 1 in-flight, 1/1 workers alive` until the new
attempt was preempted by hand.
[^2]: an earlier version of this PR fenced the old attempt with an
incarnation token on `pull_task` and `heartbeat`. It needed checks on
more RPCs: a replaced attempt that exits calls `deregister_worker` with
the shared ID, which removed the current attempt's registration.

commits.message:
Bound Zephyr shuffle buffers and export execution counters (#9884)

Bound shuffle input buffers by serialized payload size and row count, so
wide records reach the memory-aware writer before accumulating in
memory. Stream execution result serialization directly to storage.

Export live and completed coordinator counters to Finelog under the

commits.author: himanshk96
commits.message:
[dedup] Drop singletons before the fuzzy-dedup attribute shuffle (#9845)

Drop singleton documents before the fuzzy-dedup attribute shuffle
instead of
in its reducer. The final stage grouped every document by source shard
and
discarded singletons only after the shuffle, although singletons are the
large majority of documents. Singletons are now dropped on the map side
with
the same counter, and one sentinel row per source shard rides on the
first
map shard so a shard whose documents are all singletons still produces
its
empty attribute file; the reducer skips the sentinel and is otherwise
unchanged.

Attribute trees, rows, row order, schemas and counters are identical to
the
previous stage on the test corpus, on synthetic single- and multi-source
corpora including an all-singleton shard, and on a run capped at one
connected-components iteration. One intended difference: a source shard
with
zero documents now also produces an empty attribute file, where before
it
produced none; consumers that resolve every shard to an attribute path
need
the file either way.

On 1.5M nodes with 88% singletons across 200 source shards under the
local
client with eight workers:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| stage wall | 16 to 20 s | 5.5 to 6.5 s |
| rows shuffled | 1,500,000 | 180,200 |
| scatter payload | 226 MiB | 24 MiB |
| peak worker memory | 1.9 to 2.0 GiB | 1.1 to 1.3 GiB |

The dedup suite passes unchanged.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[grafana] Bound bridge memory during queries and pod scans (#9854)

Release query inputs when a cached failure is recorded, and allow at
most two dashboard computations, with each slot held from source loading
through projection. Cached errors preserve their message and HTTP
classification without retaining traceback locals or response bodies.
Arrow cache accounting includes full referenced buffers.

Stream Kubernetes pod scans one page at a time and query watched
deployments directly for the control-plane crashloop alert. Malformed
Kubernetes JSON responses produce HTTP upstream failures rather than
partial results. Keep Grafana's Cloud Run memory limit at 4 GiB in
Pulumi.

The incident exhausted both the previous 2 GiB limit and a 4 GiB
replacement. Local reproductions retained 192 MiB through failed queries
in a cache capped at 128 MiB; the change releases those tables. A
2,500-pod synthetic scan fell from 108 MiB to 32 MiB peak Python
allocations with identical results. These reproductions establish memory
defects; they do not identify every contributor to the production OOMs.

[Incident and reproduction
details](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/655).

---------

commits.author: penfever
commits.message:
Allow Atlas verifier resolutions without a separate revision (#9872)

Allow Task Trove sources to resolve confirmed verifier defects when the
resolution review explicitly records a null verifier revision. Their
graders are bundled with the dataset, so these sources have no separate
verifier-code revision. The previous SQL equality check rejected
matching null revisions.

Keep the required verifier-revision field, matching current dataset and
verifier revisions, a review timestamp after the defect was recorded,
and verified native execution. The PostgreSQL regression test fails on
main and passes with the fix; it also rejects an omitted
verifier-revision field and mismatched dataset or verifier revisions.

commits.message:
[iris] Temporarily restore legacy gVisor submissions (#9855)

Temporarily accept the deprecated GVISOR container profile (wire value
5) so already-running clients can continue submitting jobs after the
sandbox rollout. Preserve its gVisor runtime, workspace bundles,
inherited environment, cluster credentials, shared caches,

[taskcompendium] Add typed grading and remove Harbor execution (#9608)

Grade completed attempts synchronously through typed text, JSON, action,
and environment-state submissions. GradingAttempt carries the
conversation, captured file bytes, and optional state, so submission
conventions extract evidence without accessing a live workspace. Keep
JSON answers and captured environment state as separate types; both use

errors. Schema 0.22 adds the JSON answer kind and rejects serialized
TaskCompendium contracts from earlier schema versions.

Preserve the curation pipelines and runtime file grading, including
script-verifier statuses and details. Provider tool arguments are
decoded into typed conversation events at ingestion, with duplicate JSON
keys rejected.

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Benchmark the June Snowball trainer on synthetic tokens (#9693)

`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` runs the June
67B-A2B recipe's own trainer and model on synthetic tokens from one
Slurm node, with no Fray or Iris, so the Grug code path can be measured
on AMD GPUs (#9462) against Levanter's `SnowballConfig`. It builds the
production model through the recipe's width heuristic with the cooldown
launch's switches, feeds fresh uniform-random examples through
`LmDataConfig` with a mixture block the length of the dataset so nothing
repeats and the loss stays a leak check, and takes the same flags as the
Snowball harness: presets, steps, batch, expert axis, mixed-precision
policy, attention and MoE implementation, and a profile window.

The June trainer always created a checkpointer and force-saved the final
state, about 1 TB for the 67B model. `GrugTrainerConfig` gains
`save_checkpoints`; False skips the checkpointer entirely.

Measured on the AMD HPC Fund cluster at the full 67B shape on 8 GPUs,
one 4096-token sequence per GPU, bf16 or fp16 compute with f32 params:
MI350X bf16 FSDP 9.57 s per step (0.29% MFU), MI350X fp16
expert-parallel 1.09 s (2.59%), MI350X bf16 expert-parallel with the
Triton `ragged_dot` 0.73 s (3.86%), MI300X bf16 FSDP 2.27 s (2.19%),
MI300X bf16 expert-parallel about 0.76 s (6.5%). These agree with
Levanter's `SnowballConfig` through the #9613 harness within about 10%.
Details are in the baseline comment on #9462.

Part of #9462
